Whatever associating with them, constantly associating with them, intimately associating with them, repeatedly associating with them, keeping company with them, intimately keeping company with them, devotion to them, great devotion to them, and the state of being inclined towards them—this is called 'having bad friends'.

(31. Ka) assaddhiyaṃ

(31. Ka) Lack of faith

932. Tattha katamaṃ assaddhiyaṃ? Idhekacco assaddho hoti, na saddahati buddhaṃ vā dhammaṃ vā saṅghaṃ vā, yaṃ evarūpaṃ assaddhiyaṃ assaddahanā anokappanā anabhippasādo – idaṃ vuccati “assaddhiyaṃ”.

932. Herein, what is lack of faith? Here, in this Dispensation, a certain person is faithless; he does not have faith in the Buddha, or the Dhamma, or the Sangha. Whatever such lack of faith, not having faith, lack of trust, and lack of clear confidence there is—this is called 'lack of faith'.

(Kha) avadaññutā

(Kha) Ungenerosity

Tattha [T 0.0502] katamā avadaññutā? Pañca macchariyāni – āvāsamacchariyaṃ, kulamacchariyaṃ, lābhamacchariyaṃ, vaṇṇamacchariyaṃ, dhammamacchariyaṃ. Yaṃ evarūpaṃ maccheraṃ maccharāyanā maccharāyitattaṃ vevicchaṃ kadariyaṃ kaṭukañcukatā aggahitattaṃ cittassa – ayaṃ vuccati “avadaññutā”.

Herein, what is ungenerosity? There are five kinds of miserliness: miserliness regarding dwellings, families, gains, appearance, and the Dhamma. Whatever such miserliness, the manner of being miserly, the state of being miserly, stinginess, niggardliness, acridness, and a grasping state of mind there is—this is called 'ungenerosity'.

(Ga) kosajjaṃ

(Ga) Idleness

Tattha [V 0.0433] katamaṃ kosajjaṃ? Kāyaduccarite vā vacīduccarite vā manoduccarite vā pañcasu vā kāmaguṇesu cittassa vossaggo, vossaggānuppadānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ, bhāvanāya asakkaccakiriyatā asātaccakiriyatā anaṭṭhitakiriyatā olīnavuttitā nikkhittachandatā [P 0.0372] nikkhittadhuratā anāsevanā abhāvanā abahulīkammaṃ anadhiṭṭhānaṃ ananuyogo pamādo – idaṃ vuccati “kosajjaṃ”.

Herein, what is laziness? It is the letting go of the mind in regard to bodily, verbal, or mental misconduct, or in regard to the five strands of sensual pleasure, and giving in to that letting go; for the development of wholesome states, it is not acting respectfully, not acting persistently, not acting to completion, a shrinking disposition, having cast off desire, having cast off the burden, non-cultivation, non-development, not practicing it frequently, lack of resolve, lack of application, and negligence—this is called 'laziness'.

(32. Ka) uddhaccaṃ

(32. a) Restlessness

933. Tattha katamaṃ uddhaccaṃ? Yaṃ cittassa uddhaccaṃ avūpasamo cetaso vikkhepo bhavantattaṃ cittassa – idaṃ vuccati “uddhaccaṃ”.

933. Herein, what is restlessness? Whatever is the mind's restlessness, lack of calm, mental distraction, and the mind's agitation—this is called 'restlessness'.

(Kha) asaṃvaro

(b) Lack of restraint

Tattha katamo asaṃvaro? Idhekacco cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā nimittaggāhī hoti anubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya na paṭipajjati, na rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye na saṃvaraṃ āpajjati. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya nimittaggāhī hoti anubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ manindriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā [T 0.0503] dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya [M 0.0387] na paṭipajjati, na rakkhati manindriyaṃ, manindriye na saṃvaraṃ āpajjati – ayaṃ vuccati “asaṃvaro”.

Herein, what is lack of restraint? Here, a certain person, having seen a form with the eye, grasps its signs and features. Because he dwells with the eye faculty unrestrained, covetousness and displeasure, which are evil, unwholesome states, might assail him. He does not practice for its restraint, does not guard the eye faculty, and does not achieve restraint in the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear... and so on... having smelled an odor with the nose... and so on... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... and so on... having touched a tangible object with the body... and so on... having cognized a mental object with the mind, he grasps its signs and features. Because he dwells with the mind faculty unrestrained, covetousness and displeasure, which are evil, unwholesome states, might assail him. He does not practice for its restraint, does not guard the mind faculty, and does not achieve restraint in the mind faculty. This is called 'lack of restraint'.

(Ga) dussīlyaṃ

(c) Immorality

Tattha katamaṃ dussīlyaṃ? Kāyiko vītikkamo, vācasiko vītikkamo, kāyikavācasiko vītikkamo – idaṃ vuccati “dussīlyaṃ”.

Herein, what is immorality? Bodily transgression, verbal transgression, and bodily and verbal transgression—this is called 'immorality'.

(33. Ka) ariyānaṃ adassanakamyatā

(33. a) Unwillingness to see the noble ones

934. Tattha [V 0.0434] katamā ariyānaṃ adassanakamyatā? Tattha katame ariyā? Ariyā vuccanti buddhā ca buddhasāvakā ca. Yā imesaṃ ariyānaṃ adassanakamyatā adaṭṭhukamyatā asametukamyatā asamāgantukamyatā – ayaṃ vuccati “ariyānaṃ adassanakamyatā”.

934. Herein, what is unwillingness to see the noble ones? Herein, who are the noble ones? The noble ones are said to be the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas. Whatever unwillingness there is to see these noble ones, unwillingness to behold them, unwillingness to meet them, unwillingness to approach them—this is called 'unwillingness to see the noble ones'.

(Kha) saddhammaṃ asotukamyatā

(b) Unwillingness to hear the good Dhamma

Tattha katamā saddhammaṃ asotukamyatā? Tattha katamo saddhammo? Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo – ayaṃ vuccati “saddhammo”. Yā imassa saddhammassa asotukamyatā asavanakamyatā anuggahetukamyatā adhāretukamyatā – ayaṃ vuccati “saddhammaṃ asotukamyatā”.

Herein, what is unwillingness to hear the good Dhamma? Herein, what is the good Dhamma? The four establishments of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—this is called the 'good Dhamma.' Whatever unwillingness there is to hear this good Dhamma, unwillingness to listen to it, unwillingness to learn it, unwillingness to retain it—this is called 'unwillingness to hear the good Dhamma'.

(Ga) upārambhacittatā

(c) Reproachfulness

Tattha katamā upārambhacittatā? Tattha [P 0.0373] katamo upārambho? Yo upārambho anupārambho upārambhanā anupārambhanā anupārambhitattaṃ uññā avaññā paribhavo randhagavesitā – ayaṃ vuccati “upārambhacittatā”.

Herein, what is reproachfulness? Herein, what is reproach? Whatever reproach, repeated reproach, the act of reproaching, the act of repeated reproaching, the state of being repeatedly reproachful, disdain, contempt, scorn, and fault-finding there is—this is called 'reproachfulness'.

(34. Ka) muṭṭhassaccaṃ

(34. a) Forgetfulness

935. Tattha katamaṃ muṭṭhassaccaṃ? Yā assati ananussati appaṭissati assati assaraṇatā adhāraṇatā pilāpanatā sammusanatā – idaṃ vuccati “muṭṭhassaccaṃ”.

935. Herein, what is forgetfulness? Whatever lack of mindfulness, non-recollection, non-repeated-recollection, lack of mindfulness, a state of not remembering, a state of not retaining, a state of lapsing, and a state of confusion there is—this is called 'forgetfulness'.

(Kha) asampajaññaṃ

(b) Lack of clear comprehension

Tattha katamaṃ asampajaññaṃ? Yaṃ aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ [T 0.0504] …pe… avijjālaṅgī moho akusalamūlaṃ – idaṃ vuccati “asampajaññaṃ”.

Herein, what is lack of clear comprehension? Whatever not-knowing, not-seeing… and so on… the bolt of ignorance, delusion, which is an unwholesome root—this is called 'lack of clear comprehension'.

(Ga) cetaso vikkhepo

(c) Distraction of mind

Tattha [V 0.0435] katamo cetaso vikkhepo? Yaṃ cittassa uddhaccaṃ avūpasamo cetaso vikkhepo bhantattaṃ cittassa – ayaṃ vuccati “cetaso vikkhepo”.

Herein, what is distraction of mind? Whatever restlessness of mind, lack of calm, distraction of mind, and state of bewilderment of mind there is—this is called 'distraction of mind'.

(35. Ka) ayoniso manasikāro

(35. a) Unwise attention

936. Tattha katamo ayoniso manasikāro? Anicce “nicca”nti ayoniso manasikāro, dukkhe “sukha”nti ayoniso manasikāro, anattani “attā”ti ayoniso manasikāro, asubhe [M 0.0388] “subha”nti ayoniso manasikāro, saccavippaṭikulena vā cittassa āvaṭṭanā anāvaṭṭanā ābhogo samannāhāro manasikāro – ayaṃ vuccati “ayoniso manasikāro”.

936. Herein, what is unwise attention? Unwise attention to the impermanent as 'permanent'; unwise attention to suffering as 'happiness'; unwise attention to not-self as 'self'; unwise attention to the foul as 'beautiful'; or the mind's turning, repeated turning, engagement, application, and attention in a way contrary to truth—this is called 'unwise attention'.

(Kha) kummaggasevanā

(b) Cultivation of a wrong path

Tattha katamā kummaggasevanā? Tattha katamo kummaggo? Micchādiṭṭhi, micchāsaṅkappo, micchāvācā, micchākammanto, micchāājīvo, micchāvāyāmo, micchāsati, micchāsamādhi – ayaṃ vuccati “kummaggo”. Yā imassa kummaggassa sevanā nisevanā saṃsevanā bhajanā sambhajanā bhatti sambhatti taṃsampavaṅkatā – ayaṃ vuccati “kummaggasevanā”.

Herein, what is the cultivation of a wrong path? Herein, what is a wrong path? Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration—this is called a 'wrong path.' Whatever cultivation of this wrong path, firm cultivation, thorough cultivation, association, thorough association, devotion, thorough devotion, and inclination towards it there is—this is called 'the cultivation of a wrong path'.

(Ga) cetaso ca līnattaṃ

(c) And sluggishness of mind

Tattha katamaṃ cetaso ca līnattaṃ? Yā cittassa akalyatā akammaññatā olīyanā sallīyanā līnaṃ līyanā līyitattaṃ thinaṃ thiyanā thiyitattaṃ cittassa – idaṃ vuccati “cetaso ca līnattaṃ”.

Herein, what is and sluggishness of mind? Whatever unfitness of mind, unworkability, clinging, thorough clinging, shrinking, the manner of shrinking, the state of being shrunken, torpor, the manner of being torpid, and the state of being torpid of mind there is—this is called 'and sluggishness of mind'.

Tikaṃ.

The Triad.

4. Catukkaniddeso

4. Exposition of the Fours

(1) Cattāro āsavā

(1) The Four Taints

937. Tattha [V 0.0436] katame cattāro āsavā? Kāmāsavo, bhavāsavo, diṭṭhāsavo, avijjāsavo.

937. Herein, what are the four taints? The taint of sensual pleasure, the taint of becoming, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.

(Ka) kāmāsavo

(a) The Taint of Sensual Pleasure

Tattha katamo kāmāsavo? Yo [P 0.0374] kāmesu kāmacchando [T 0.0505] kāmarāgo kāmanandī kāmataṇhā kāmasineho kāmapariḷāho kāmamucchā kāmajjhosānaṃ – ayaṃ vuccati “kāmāsavo”.

Herein, what is the taint of sensual pleasure? Whatever desire for sensual pleasures, lust for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, craving for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, fever for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, and obsession with sensual pleasures—this is called the 'taint of sensual pleasure'.

(Kha) bhavāsavo

(b) The Taint of Becoming

Tattha katamo bhavāsavo? Yo bhavesu bhavacchando…pe… bhavajjhosānaṃ – ayaṃ vuccati “bhavāsavo”.

Herein, what is the taint of becoming? Whatever desire for becoming... and so on... obsession with becoming—this is called the 'taint of becoming'.

(Ga) diṭṭhāsavo

(c) The Taint of Views

Tattha katamo diṭṭhāsavo? “Sassato loko”ti vā, “asassato loko”ti vā, “antavā loko”ti vā, “anantavā loko”ti vā, “taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”nti vā, “aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra”nti vā, “hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti vā, “na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti vā, “hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti vā, “neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti vā. Yā evarūpā diṭṭhi [M 0.0389] diṭṭhigataṃ…pe… vipariyāsaggāho – ayaṃ vuccati “diṭṭhāsavo”. Sabbāpi micchādiṭṭhi diṭṭhāsavo.

Therein, what is the taint of views? Such views as: 'The world is eternal,' or 'the world is not eternal'; 'the world is finite,' or 'the world is infinite'; 'the life-principle and the body are the same,' or 'the life-principle is one thing and the body another'; 'a being exists after death,' or 'a being does not exist after death,' or 'a being both exists and does not exist after death,' or 'a being neither exists nor does not exist after death.' Whatever such view, holding to a view... and so on... perverse grasping—this is called the taint of views. All wrong view is the taint of views.

(Gha) avijjāsavo

(d) The Taint of Ignorance

Tattha katamo avijjāsavo? Dukkhe aññāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudaye aññāṇaṃ[V 0.0437], dukkhanirodhe aññāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya aññāṇaṃ, pubbante aññāṇaṃ, aparante aññāṇaṃ, pubbantāparante aññāṇaṃ, idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu aññāṇaṃ. Yaṃ evarūpaṃ aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ…pe… avijjālaṅgī moho akusalamūlaṃ – ayaṃ vuccati “avijjāsavo”. Ime cattāro āsavā.

Therein, what is the taint of ignorance? Ignorance concerning suffering, ignorance concerning the origin of suffering, ignorance concerning the cessation of suffering, ignorance concerning the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering; ignorance concerning the past, ignorance concerning the future, ignorance concerning the past and the future; ignorance concerning specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena. Whatever such ignorance, not seeing... and so on... the bolt of ignorance, delusion, the unwholesome root—this is called the taint of ignorance. These are the four taints.

(2-5) Cattāro ganthādī

(2–5) The Four Bonds, etc.

938. Tattha katame cattāro ganthā [P 0.0375] …pe… [T 0.0506] cattāro oghā…pe… cattāro yogā…pe… cattāri upādānāni? Kāmupādānaṃ, diṭṭhupādānaṃ, sīlabbatupādānaṃ, attavādupādānaṃ.

938. Therein, what are the four bonds? ...and so on... the four floods? ...and so on... the four yokes? ...and so on... the four kinds of clinging? Clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rites and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self.

(Ka) kāmupādānaṃ

(a) Clinging to Sensual Pleasures

Tattha katamaṃ kāmupādānaṃ? Yo kāmesu kāmacchando…pe… kāmajjhosānaṃ – idaṃ vuccati “kāmupādānaṃ”.

Therein, what is clinging to sensual pleasures? Whatever desire for sensual pleasures... and so on... obsession with sensual pleasures—this is called clinging to sensual pleasures.

(Kha) diṭṭhupādānaṃ

(b) Clinging to views

Tattha katamaṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ? “Natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ…pe… ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī”ti. Yā evarūpā diṭṭhi diṭṭhigataṃ…pe… vipariyāsaggāho – idaṃ vuccati “diṭṭhupādānaṃ”. Ṭhapetvā sīlabbatupādānañca attavādupādānañca sabbāpi micchādiṭṭhi diṭṭhupādānaṃ.

Therein, what is clinging to views? ‘There is nothing given, there is nothing sacrificed... there are no ascetics and brahmins who, having directly known and realized for themselves this world and the next, make it known.’ Whatever view of such a kind, a tenet of view... a perverse grasping—this is called ‘clinging to views’. Setting aside clinging to rites and observances and clinging to the doctrine of self, all other wrong view is clinging to views.

(Ga) sīlabbatupādānaṃ

(c) Clinging to rites and observances

Tattha katamaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ? Ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlena suddhi vatena suddhi sīlabbatena suddhīti. Yā evarūpā diṭṭhi diṭṭhigataṃ…pe… vipariyāsaggāho – idaṃ vuccati “sīlabbatupādānaṃ”.

Therein, what is clinging to rites and observances? It is the view of ascetics and brahmins outside this Dispensation that ‘purification is through a rite, purification is through an observance, purification is through a rite and observance.’ Whatever view of such a kind, a tenet of view... a perverse grasping—this is called ‘clinging to rites and observances’.

(Gha) attavādupādānaṃ

(d) Clinging to a doctrine of self

Tattha [V 0.0438] katamaṃ attavādupādānaṃ? Idha assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto – rūpaṃ attato samanupassati rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ [T 0.0507] attani vā rūpaṃ rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Vedanaṃ…pe… saññaṃ…pe… saṅkhāre…pe… viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ attani vā viññāṇaṃ viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Yā evarūpā diṭṭhi diṭṭhigataṃ…pe… vipariyāsaggāho – idaṃ vuccati “attavādupādānaṃ”. Imāni cattāri upādānāni.

Therein, what is clinging to a doctrine of self? Here, an uninstructed worldling, who is not a seer of the noble ones, unskilled and undisciplined in the noble Dhamma; who is not a seer of true persons, unskilled and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He regards feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. Whatever view of such a kind, a tenet of view... a perverse grasping—this is called ‘clinging to a doctrine of self’. These are the four clingings.

(6) Cattāro taṇhuppādā

(6) The four arisings of craving

939. Tattha [M 0.0390] katame cattāro taṇhuppādā? Cīvarahetu vā bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, piṇḍapātahetu vā bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, senāsanahetu vā bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, itibhavābhavahetu vā bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati – ime cattāro taṇhuppādā.

939. Therein, what are the four arisings of craving? Craving arises in a bhikkhu on account of a robe; craving arises in a bhikkhu on account of almsfood; craving arises in a bhikkhu on account of a lodging; craving arises in a bhikkhu on account of this or that state of existence. These are the four arisings of craving.

(7) Cattāri agatigamanāni

(7) The four wrong courses

Tattha katamāni cattāri agatigamanāni? Chandāgatiṃ [P 0.0376] gacchati, dosāgatiṃ gacchati, mohāgatiṃ gacchati, bhayāgatiṃ gacchati. Yā evarūpā agati agatigamanaṃ chandagamanaṃ vaggagamanaṃ vārigamanaṃ – imāni cattāri agatigamanāni.

Therein, what are the four wrong courses? One follows a wrong course out of desire; one follows a wrong course out of hatred; one follows a wrong course out of delusion; one follows a wrong course out of fear. Any such wrong course, taking a wrong course, going by desire, partiality, or deviation—these are the four wrong courses.

(8) Cattāro vipariyāsā

(8) The four distortions

Tattha [V 0.0439] katame cattāro vipariyāsā? Anicce “nicca”nti saññāvipariyāso cittavipariyāso diṭṭhivipariyāso, dukkhe “sukha”nti saññāvipariyāso cittavipariyāso diṭṭhivipariyāso, anattani “attā”ti saññāvipariyāso cittavipariyāso diṭṭhivipariyāso, asubhe “subha”nti saññāvipariyāso cittavipariyāso diṭṭhivipariyāso – ime cattāro vipariyāsā.

Therein, what are the four distortions? With regard to the impermanent, the distortion of perception, distortion of mind, and distortion of view that it is 'permanent.' With regard to what is suffering, the distortion of perception, distortion of mind, and distortion of view that it is 'happiness.' With regard to what is not-self, the distortion of perception, distortion of mind, and distortion of view that it is 'self.' With regard to the foul, the distortion of perception, distortion of mind, and distortion of view that it is 'beautiful.' These are the four distortions.

(9) Cattāro anariyavohārā

(9) The four ignoble usages

Tattha [T 0.0508] katame cattāro anariyavohārā? Adiṭṭhe diṭṭhavāditā, assute sutavāditā, amute mutavāditā, aviññāte viññātavāditā – ime cattāro anariyavohārā.

Therein, what are the four ignoble usages? Regarding the unseen, speaking of it as seen; regarding the unheard, speaking of it as heard; regarding the unsensed, speaking of it as sensed; regarding the uncognized, speaking of it as cognized. These are the four ignoble usages.

(10) Aparepi cattāro anariyavohārā

(10) Another four ignoble usages

Tattha katame aparepi cattāro anariyavohārā? Diṭṭhe adiṭṭhavāditā, sute assutavāditā, mute amutavāditā, viññāte aviññātavāditā – ime cattāro anariyavohārā.

Therein, what are the other four ignoble usages? Regarding the seen, speaking of it as unseen; regarding the heard, speaking of it as unheard; regarding the sensed, speaking of it as unsensed; regarding the cognized, speaking of it as uncognized. These are the four ignoble usages.

(11) Cattāri duccaritāni

(11) The four kinds of misconduct

Tattha katamāni cattāri duccaritāni? Pāṇātipāto, adinnādānaṃ, kāmesumicchācāro, musāvādo – imāni cattāri duccaritāni.

Therein, what are the four kinds of misconduct? The destruction of life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech. These are the four kinds of misconduct.

(12) Aparānipi cattāri duccaritāni

(12) Another four kinds of misconduct

Tattha katamāni aparānipi cattāri duccaritāni? Musāvādo, pisuṇā vācā, pharusā vācā, samphappalāpo – imāni cattāri duccaritāni.

Therein, what are the other four kinds of misconduct? False speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter. These are the four kinds of misconduct.

(13) Cattāri bhayāni

(13) The four fears

Tattha katamāni cattāri bhayāni? Jātibhayaṃ, jarābhayaṃ, byādhibhayaṃ, maraṇabhayaṃ – imāni cattāri bhayāni.

Therein, what are the four fears? The fear of birth, the fear of aging, the fear of illness, and the fear of death. These are the four fears.

(14) Aparānipi cattāri bhayāni

(14) Another four fears

Tattha [V 0.0440] katamāni aparānipi cattāri bhayāni? Rājabhayaṃ, corabhayaṃ, aggibhayaṃ, udakabhayaṃ – imāni cattāri bhayāni.

Herein, what are the other four fears? The fear of kings, the fear of thieves, the fear of fire, and the fear of water. These are the four fears.

Tattha [M 0.0391] katamāni aparānipi cattāri bhayāni? Ūmibhayaṃ, kumbhīlabhayaṃ kumbhīrabhayaṃ, kumbhīḷabhayaṃ (?) (kumbha + īra + a = bhaya), āvaṭṭabhayaṃ, susukābhayaṃ – imāni cattāri bhayāni.

Herein, what are another four fears? The fear of waves, the fear of crocodiles, the fear of whirlpools, and the fear of sharks. These are the four fears.

Tattha katamāni aparānipi cattāri bhayāni? Attānuvādabhayaṃ, parānuvādabhayaṃ, daṇḍabhayaṃ, duggatibhayaṃ – imāni cattāri bhayāni.

Herein, what are the other four fears? The fear of self-reproach, the fear of reproach by others, the fear of punishment, and the fear of a bad destination. These are the four fears.

(15) Catasso diṭṭhiyo

(15) Four Views.

Tattha [T 0.0509] katamā catasso diṭṭhiyo? “Sayaṅkataṃ sukhadukkha”nti saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati, “paraṅkataṃ sukhadukkha”nti saccato thetato diṭṭhi [P 0.0377] uppajjati, “sayaṅkatañca paraṅkatañca sukhadukkha”nti saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati, “asayaṅkāraṃ aparaṅkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ sukhadukkha”nti saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati – imā catasso diṭṭhiyo.

Herein, what are the four views? The view arises, as true and certain, that 'pleasure and pain are self-made.' The view arises, as true and certain, that 'pleasure and pain are made by another.' The view arises, as true and certain, that 'pleasure and pain are both self-made and made by another.' The view arises, as true and certain, that 'pleasure and pain are not self-made, not other-made, but have arisen without a cause.' These are the four views.

Catukkaṃ.

The Tetrad.

5. Pañcakaniddeso

5. Exposition of the Fives

(1) Pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni

(1) The Five Lower Fetters.

940. Tattha katamāni pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni? Sakkāyadiṭṭhi, vicikicchā, sīlabbataparāmāso, kāmacchando, byāpādo – imāni pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni.

940. Herein, what are the five lower fetters? Identity view, doubt, clinging to rules and observances, sensual desire, and ill will—these are the five lower fetters.

(2) Pañcuddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni

(2) The Five Higher Fetters.

Tattha katamāni pañcuddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni? Rūparāgo, arūparāgo, māno, uddhaccaṃ, avijjā – imāni pañcuddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni.

Herein, what are the five higher fetters? Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance—these are the five higher fetters.

(3) Pañca macchariyāni

(3) Five Kinds of Stinginess.

Tattha [V 0.0441] katamāni pañca macchariyāni? Āvāsamacchariyaṃ, kulamacchariyaṃ, lābhamacchariyaṃ, vaṇṇamacchariyaṃ, dhammamacchariyaṃ – imāni pañca macchariyāni.

Herein, what are the five kinds of stinginess? Stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding beauty, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma—these are the five kinds of stinginess.

(4) Pañca saṅgā

(4) Five Thorns.

Tattha katame pañca saṅgā? Rāgasaṅgo, dosasaṅgo, mohasaṅgo, mānasaṅgo, diṭṭhisaṅgo – ime pañca saṅgā.

Herein, what are the five thorns? The thorn of lust, the thorn of hatred, the thorn of delusion, the thorn of conceit, and the thorn of views—these are the five thorns.

(5) Pañca sallā

(5) Five Darts.

Tattha katame pañca sallā? Rāgasallaṃ, dosasallaṃ, mohasallaṃ, mānasallaṃ, diṭṭhisallaṃ – ime pañca sallā.

Herein, what are the five darts? The dart of lust, the dart of hatred, the dart of delusion, the dart of conceit, and the dart of views—these are the five darts.

(6) Pañca cetokhilā

(6) Five Stakes of the Mind.

941. Tattha katame pañca cetokhilā? Satthari kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati [T 0.0510] na sampasīdati, dhamme kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati, saṅghe [M 0.0392] kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati, sikkhāya kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati, sabrahmacārīsu kupito hoti anattamano āhatacitto khilajāto – ime pañca cetokhilā.

941. Herein, what are the five stakes of the mind? Regarding the Teacher, one doubts, is uncertain, is not resolved, and is not confident. Regarding the Dhamma, one doubts, is uncertain, is not resolved, and is not confident. Regarding the Saṅgha, one doubts, is uncertain, is not resolved, and is not confident. Regarding the training, one doubts, is uncertain, is not resolved, and is not confident. Towards one's companions in the holy life, one is angry, displeased, has an afflicted mind, and becomes obstinate like a stake. These are the five stakes of the mind.

(7) Pañca cetaso vinibandhā

(7) Five Shackles of the Mind.

Tattha katame pañca cetaso vinibandhā? Kāme avītarāgo hoti avigatacchando avigatapemo avigatapipāso avigatapariḷāho avigatataṇho; kāye avītarāgo hoti… rūpe avītarāgo hoti… yāvadatthaṃ [P 0.0378] udarāvadehakaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhaṃ passasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ anuyutto viharati; aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ carati – “imināhaṃ sīlena vā [V 0.0442] vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā”ti – ime pañca cetasovinibandhā.

Herein, what are the five shackles of the mind? (1) One is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, with desire, affection, thirst, fever, and craving for them unallayed; (2) one is not free from lust for one's own body…; (3) one is not free from lust for external forms…; (4) having eaten one’s fill, one dwells devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of sleeping on one's side, and the pleasure of sleep; (5) one lives the holy life aspiring to be reborn in some order of gods, thinking: ‘By this morality or observance or austerity or holy life I will become a great god or a lesser god.’ These are the five shackles of the mind.

(8) Pañca nīvaraṇāni

(8) The Five Hindrances.

Tattha katamāni pañca nīvaraṇāni? Kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ, byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ, thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ, uddhaccakukkuccanīvaraṇaṃ, vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ – imāni pañca nīvaraṇāni.

Herein, what are the five hindrances? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt—these are the five hindrances.

(9) Pañca kammāni ānantarikāni

(9) The Five Deeds with Immediate Result.

Tattha katamāni pañca kammāni ānantarikāni? Mātā jīvitā voropitā hoti, pitā jīvitā voropito hoti, arahanto jīvitā voropito hoti, duṭṭhena cittena tathāgatassa lohitaṃ uppāditaṃ hoti[T 0.0511], saṅgho bhinno hoti – imāni pañca kammāni ānantarikāni.

Herein, what are the five deeds with immediate result? One has deprived one’s mother of life; one has deprived one’s father of life; one has deprived an arahant of life; with a corrupt mind, one has caused the blood of a Tathāgata to be shed; one has split the Saṅgha. These are the five deeds with immediate result.

(10) Pañca diṭṭhiyo

(10) Five Views.

Tattha katamā pañca diṭṭhiyo? “Saññī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti ittheke abhivadanti, “asaññī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti ittheke abhivadanti, “nevasaññīnāsaññī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti ittheke abhivadanti, sato vā pana sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññāpenti, diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ vā paneke abhivadanti – imā pañca diṭṭhiyo.

Herein, what are the five views? Some assert: ‘The self is percipient and permanent after death.’ Some assert: ‘The self is non-percipient and permanent after death.’ Some assert: ‘The self is neither percipient nor non-percipient and permanent after death.’ Others proclaim the cutting off, destruction, and non-becoming of an existing being. Still others assert Nibbāna in this very life. These are the five views.

(11) Pañca verā

(11) Five Enmities.

942. Tattha katame pañca verā? Pāṇātipāto, adinnādānaṃ, kāmesumicchācāro, musāvādo, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā – ime pañca verā.

942. Herein, what are the five enmities? Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and indulgence in liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are a basis for heedlessness—these are the five enmities.

(12) Pañca byasanā

(12) Five Misfortunes.

Tattha [M 0.0393][V 0.0443] katame pañca byasanā? Ñātibyasanaṃ, bhogabyasanaṃ, rogabyasanaṃ, sīlabyasanaṃ, diṭṭhibyasanaṃ – ime pañca byasanā.

Herein, what are the five misfortunes? The misfortune of relatives, the misfortune of wealth, the misfortune of illness, the misfortune of virtue, and the misfortune of view—these are the five misfortunes.

(13) Pañca akkhantiyā ādīnavā

(13) The five drawbacks of impatience.

Tattha katame pañca akkhantiyā ādīnavā? Bahuno janassa appiyo hoti amanāpo, verabahulo ca hoti, vajjabahulo ca, sammūḷho kālaṅkaroti, kāyassa bhedā [P 0.0379] paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati – ime pañca akkhantiyā ādīnavā.

Herein, what are the five drawbacks of impatience? One is unloved and disagreeable to many people, abounding in enmity, abounding in blame, one dies bewildered, and with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. These are the five drawbacks of impatience.

(14) Pañca bhayāni

(14) The five fears.

Tattha katamāni pañca bhayāni? Ājīvakabhayaṃ, asilokabhayaṃ, parisasārajjabhayaṃ, maraṇabhayaṃ, duggatibhayaṃ – imāni pañca bhayāni.

Herein, what are the five fears? The fear concerning livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of timidity in assemblies, the fear of death, and the fear of a bad destination. These are the five fears.

(15) Pañca diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā

(15) The five doctrines of Nibbāna in this present life.

943. Tattha katame pañca diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā?

943. Herein, what are the five doctrines of Nibbāna in this present life?

(Ka) idhekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī hoti evaṃdiṭṭhi evaṃdiṭṭhi (syā.) – “yato kho, bho[T 0.0512], ayaṃ attā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāreti, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti.

(a) Here, a certain ascetic or brahmin has such a doctrine and view: ‘Sirs, when this self indulges, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, to that extent, sirs, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this present life.’ In this way, some declare the supreme Nibbāna in this present life for an existing being.

(Kha) tamañño evamāha – “atthi kho, bho, eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi neso natthīti vadāmi. No ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto hoti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Kāmā hi, bho, aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā. Tesaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā [V 0.0444] vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti.

(b) Another says to him: ‘Sirs, there is that self of which you speak. I do not say that it does not exist. But, sirs, this self has not thereby attained the supreme Nibbāna in this present life. For what reason? Because, sirs, sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. From their change and alteration, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise. Sirs, when this self, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and dwells in the first jhāna, to that extent, sirs, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this present life.’ In this way, some declare the supreme Nibbāna in this present life for an existing being.

(Ga) tamañño evamāha – “atthi kho, bho, eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi. Neso natthīti vadāmi. No ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto hoti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yadeva tattha vitakkitaṃ vicāritaṃ etena etaṃ oḷārikaṃ akkhāyati. Yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti.

(c) Another says to him: ‘Sirs, there is that self of which you speak. I do not say that it does not exist. But, sirs, this self has not thereby attained the supreme Nibbāna in this present life. For what reason? Because whatever applied thought and sustained thought is there, by that, this is declared to be gross. Sirs, when this self, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought … enters and dwells in the second jhāna, to that extent, sirs, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this present life.’ In this way, some declare the supreme Nibbāna in this present life for an existing being.

(Gha) tamañño [M 0.0394] evamāha – “atthi kho, bho, eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi. Neso natthīti vadāmi. No ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto [T 0.0513] hoti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yadeva tattha pītigataṃ cetaso uppilāvitaṃ, etena etaṃ oḷārikaṃ akkhāyati. Yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā pītiyā ca virāgā…pe… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto [P 0.0380] hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti.

(d) Another says to him: ‘Sirs, there is that self of which you speak. I do not say that it does not exist. But, sirs, this self has not thereby attained the supreme Nibbāna in this present life. For what reason? Because whatever is connected with rapture and the mind’s elation is there, by that, this is declared to be gross. Sirs, when this self, with the fading away of rapture … enters and dwells in the third jhāna, to that extent, sirs, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this present life.’ In this way, some declare the supreme Nibbāna in this present life for an existing being.

(Ṅa) tamañño evamāha – “atthi kho, bho, eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi. Neso natthīti vadāmi. No ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto hoti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yadeva tattha sukhapīti cetaso ābhogo, etena etaṃ oḷārikaṃ akkhāyati. Yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti. Ime pañca diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā.

(e) Another says to him: ‘Sirs, there is that self of which you speak. I do not say that it does not exist. But, sirs, this self has not thereby attained the supreme Nibbāna in this present life. For what reason? Because whatever pleasure and the mind’s inclination is there, by that, this is declared to be gross. Sirs, when this self, with the abandoning of pleasure … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, to that extent, sirs, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this present life.’ In this way, some declare the supreme Nibbāna in this present life for an existing being. These are the five doctrines of Nibbāna in this present life.

Pañcakaṃ.

The Pentad.

6. Chakkaniddeso

6. Exposition of the Sixes

(1) Cha vivādamūlāni

(1) The six roots of disputes.

944. Tattha [V 0.0445] katamāni cha vivādamūlāni? Kodho, makkho, issā, sāṭheyyaṃ, pāpicchatā, sandiṭṭhiparāmāsitā – imāni cha vivādamūlāni.

944. Herein, what are the six roots of disputes? Anger, contempt, envy, deceit, evil desires, and adherence to one’s own views. These are the six roots of disputes.

(2) Cha chandarāgā

(2) The six lustful desires.

Tattha katame cha chandarāgā? Chandarāgā gehasitā dhammā. Manāpiyesu rūpesu gehasito rāgo sārāgo cittassa sārāgo, manāpiyesu saddesu…pe… manāpiyesu gandhesu…pe… manāpiyesu rasesu…pe… manāpiyesu phoṭṭhabbesu…pe… manāpiyesu dhammesu gehasito rāgo [T 0.0514] sārāgo cittassa sārāgo – ime cha chandarāgā.

Herein, what are the six lustful desires? Lustful desires are states connected with the household. With regard to agreeable forms, there is household-based lust, passionate attachment, a passionate attachment of the mind; with regard to agreeable sounds… with regard to agreeable odors… with regard to agreeable tastes… with regard to agreeable tangible objects… with regard to agreeable mental phenomena, there is household-based lust, passionate attachment, a passionate attachment of the mind. These are the six lustful desires.

(3) Cha virodhavatthūni

(3) The six grounds for opposition.

Tattha katamāni cha virodhavatthūni? Amanāpiyesu rūpesu cittassa āghāto paṭighāto caṇḍikkaṃ asuropo anattamanatā cittassa, amanāpiyesu saddesu…pe… amanāpiyesu gandhesu…pe… amanāpiyesu rasesu…pe… amanāpiyesu phoṭṭhabbesu…pe… amanāpiyesu dhammesu cittassa [M 0.0395] āghāto paṭighāto caṇḍikkaṃ asuropo anattamanatā cittassa – imāni cha virodhavatthūni.

Herein, what are the six grounds for opposition? Towards disagreeable forms, there is animosity of the mind, repugnance, harshness, sullenness, and displeasure of the mind; towards disagreeable sounds… towards disagreeable odors… towards disagreeable tastes… towards disagreeable tangible objects… towards disagreeable mental phenomena, there is animosity of the mind, repugnance, harshness, sullenness, and displeasure of the mind. These are the six grounds for opposition.

(4) Cha taṇhākāyā

(4) The six bodies of craving.

Tattha katame cha taṇhākāyā? Rūpataṇhā, saddataṇhā, gandhataṇhā, rasataṇhā, phoṭṭhabbataṇhā, dhammataṇhā – ime cha taṇhākāyā.

Herein, what are the six bodies of craving? Craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangible objects, and craving for mental phenomena. These are the six bodies of craving.

(5) Cha agāravā

(5) The six kinds of disrespect.

945. Tattha [P 0.0381][V 0.0446] katame cha agāravā? Satthari agāravo viharati appatisso, dhamme agāravo viharati appatisso, saṅghe agāravo viharati appatisso, sikkhāya agāravo viharati appatisso, appamāde agāravo viharati appatisso, paṭisanthāre agāravo viharati appatisso – ime cha agāravā.

945. Herein, what are the six kinds of disrespect? One dwells disrespectful and without deference toward the Teacher; one dwells disrespectful and without deference toward the Dhamma; one dwells disrespectful and without deference toward the Saṅgha; one dwells disrespectful and without deference toward the training; one dwells disrespectful and without deference toward heedfulness; one dwells disrespectful and without deference toward cordiality. These are the six kinds of disrespect.

(6) Cha parihāniyā dhammā

(6) The six states that lead to decline.

Tattha katame cha parihāniyā dhammā? Kammārāmatā, bhassārāmatā, niddārāmatā, saṅgaṇikārāmatā, saṃsaggārāmatā, papañcārāmatā – ime cha parihāniyā dhammā.

Herein, what are the six states that lead to decline? Delight in activity, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, delight in intimacy, and delight in proliferation. These are the six states that lead to decline.

(7) Aparepi cha parihāniyā dhammā

(7) Another six states that lead to decline.

946. Tattha katame aparepi cha parihāniyā dhammā? Kammārāmatā, bhassārāmatā, niddārāmatā, saṅgaṇikārāmatā, dovacassatā, pāpamittatā – ime cha parihāniyā dhammā.

946. Herein, what are the other six states that lead to decline? Delight in activity, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, being difficult to admonish, and having bad friends. These are the six states that lead to decline.

(8) Cha somanassupavicārā

(8) Six Reflections concerning Joy

Tattha [T 0.0515] katame cha somanassupavicārā? Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ rūpaṃ upavicarati, sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ dhammaṃ upavicarati – ime cha somanassupavicārā.

Herein, what are the six reflections concerning joy? Having seen a form with the eye, one reflects upon a form that is a basis for joy; having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having touched a tangible object with the body… having cognized a mental object with the mind, one reflects upon a mental object that is a basis for joy—these are the six reflections concerning joy.

(9) Cha domanassupavicārā

(9) Six Reflections concerning Displeasure

Tattha katame cha domanassupavicārā? Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā domanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ rūpaṃ upavicarati, sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā [V 0.0447] …pe… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya domanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ dhammaṃ upavicarati – ime cha domanassupavicārā.

Herein, what are the six reflections concerning displeasure? Having seen a form with the eye, one reflects upon a form that is a basis for displeasure; having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having touched a tangible object with the body… having cognized a mental object with the mind, one reflects upon a mental object that is a basis for displeasure—these are the six reflections concerning displeasure.

(10) Cha upekkhupavicārā

(10) Six Reflections concerning Equanimity

Tattha katame cha upekkhupavicārā? Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā upekkhāṭṭhāniyaṃ rūpaṃ upavicarati, sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya upekkhāṭṭhāniyaṃ dhammaṃ upavicarati – ime cha upekkhupavicārā.

Herein, what are the six reflections concerning equanimity? Having seen a form with the eye, one reflects upon a form that is a basis for equanimity; having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having touched a tangible object with the body… having cognized a mental object with the mind, one reflects upon a mental object that is a basis for equanimity—these are the six reflections concerning equanimity.

(11) Cha gehasitāni somanassāni

(11) Six Joys Pertaining to the Household Life

947. Tattha [M 0.0396] katamāni cha gehasitāni somanassāni? Manāpiyesu rūpesu gehasitaṃ cetasikaṃ sātaṃ cetasikaṃ sukhaṃ cetosamphassajaṃ sātaṃ sukhaṃ vedayitaṃ cetosamphassajā sātā sukhā vedanā, manāpiyesu saddesu…pe… manāpiyesu gandhesu…pe… manāpiyesu rasesu…pe… manāpiyesu phoṭṭhabbesu…pe… manāpiyesu dhammesu gehasitaṃ cetasikaṃ sātaṃ cetasikaṃ sukhaṃ [T 0.0516] cetosamphassajaṃ sātaṃ sukhaṃ [P 0.0382] vedayitaṃ cetosamphassajā sātā sukhā vedanā – imāni cha gehasitāni somanassāni.

947. Herein, what are the six joys pertaining to the household life? With respect to agreeable forms, there is household-based mental pleasure, mental happiness, a pleasant happy feeling born of mind-contact, and a pleasant happy sensation born of mind-contact. With respect to agreeable sounds… with respect to agreeable smells… with respect to agreeable tastes… with respect to agreeable tangible objects… with respect to agreeable mental objects, there is household-based mental pleasure, mental happiness, a pleasant happy feeling born of mind-contact, and a pleasant happy sensation born of mind-contact. These are the six joys pertaining to the household life.

(12) Cha gehasitāni domanassāni

(12) Six Displeasures Pertaining to the Household Life

Tattha katamāni cha gehasitāni domanassāni? Amanāpiyesu rūpesu gehasitaṃ cetasikaṃ asātaṃ cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ cetosamphassajaṃ asātaṃ dukkhaṃ vedayitaṃ cetosamphassajā asātā dukkhā vedanā, amanāpiyesu saddesu…pe… amanāpiyesu gandhesu…pe… amanāpiyesu rasesu…pe… amanāpiyesu phoṭṭhabbesu…pe… amanāpiyesu dhammesu gehasitaṃ cetasikaṃ asātaṃ cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ cetosamphassajaṃ asātaṃ dukkhaṃ vedayitaṃ cetosamphassajā asātā dukkhā vedanā – imāni cha gehasitāni domanassāni.

Herein, what are the six displeasures pertaining to the household life? With respect to disagreeable forms, there is household-based mental displeasure, mental pain, an unpleasant painful feeling born of mind-contact, and an unpleasant painful sensation born of mind-contact. With respect to disagreeable sounds… with respect to disagreeable smells… with respect to disagreeable tastes… with respect to disagreeable tangible objects… with respect to disagreeable mental objects, there is household-based mental displeasure, mental pain, an unpleasant painful feeling born of mind-contact, and an unpleasant painful sensation born of mind-contact. These are the six displeasures pertaining to the household life.

(13) Cha gehasitā upekkhā

(13) Six Household-Based Equanimities

Tattha [V 0.0448] katamā cha gehasitā upekkhā? Upekkhāṭṭhāniyesu rūpesu gehasitaṃ cetasikaṃ neva sātaṃ nāsātaṃ cetosamphassajaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedayitaṃ cetosamphassajā adukkhamasukhā vedanā, upekkhāṭṭhāniyesu saddesu…pe… upekkhāṭṭhāniyesu gandhesu…pe… upekkhāṭṭhāniyesu rasesu…pe… upekkhāṭṭhāniyesu phoṭṭhabbesu…pe… upekkhāṭṭhāniyesu dhammesu gehasitaṃ cetasikaṃ neva sātaṃ nāsātaṃ cetosamphassajaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedayitaṃ cetosamphassajā adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā cha gehasitā upekkhā.

Herein, what are the six household-based equanimities? Regarding forms that are a basis for equanimity, there is a household-based mental state that is neither agreeable nor disagreeable, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mind-contact, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation born of mind-contact. Regarding sounds that are a basis for equanimity… regarding smells… regarding tastes… regarding tangibles… regarding mental objects that are a basis for equanimity, there is a household-based mental state that is neither agreeable nor disagreeable, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mind-contact, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation born of mind-contact. These are the six household-based equanimities.

(14) Cha diṭṭhiyo

(14) Six Views

948. Tattha katamā cha diṭṭhiyo? “Atthi me attā”ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati, “natthi me attā”ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati, “attanā vā attānaṃ sañjānāmī”ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati, “attanā vā anattānaṃ sañjānāmī”ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati, “anattanā vā attānaṃ sañjānāmī”ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; atha vā panassa [M 0.0397] evaṃdiṭṭhi hoti – “so me ayaṃ attā vado vedeyyo tatra tatra dīgharattaṃ kalyāṇapāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ vipākaṃ paccanubhoti. Na so jāto nāhosi, na so jāto na bhavissati, nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo”ti vā panassa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati. Imā cha diṭṭhiyo.

948. Herein, what are the six views? A view arises in one as true and established that: “I have a self”; or “I have no self”; or “By self I perceive self”; or “By self I perceive not-self”; or “By not-self I perceive self.” Or else a view such as this arises in one as true and established: “This self of mine is the speaker and the feeler who, here and there for a long time, experiences the result of good and bad actions; it was not born and did not come to be, it is not born and will not come to be; it is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change.” These are the six views.

Chakkaṃ.

The Section on Sixes.

7. Sattakaniddeso

7. Exposition of the Sevens

(1) Sattānusayā

(1) Seven Underlying Tendencies

949. Tattha [P 0.0383] katame sattānusayā? Kāmarāgānusayo, paṭighānusayo, mānānusayo, diṭṭhānusayo, vicikicchānusayo, bhavarāgānusayo, avijjānusayo – ime satta anusayā.

949. Herein, what are the seven underlying tendencies? The underlying tendency of sensual lust, the underlying tendency of aversion, the underlying tendency of conceit, the underlying tendency of views, the underlying tendency of doubt, the underlying tendency of craving for existence, and the underlying tendency of ignorance—these are the seven underlying tendencies.

(2) Satta saṃyojanāni

(2) Seven Fetters

Tattha [V 0.0449] katamāni satta saṃyojanāni? Kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ, paṭighasaṃyojanaṃ, mānasaṃyojanaṃ, diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ, vicikicchāsaṃyojanaṃ, bhavarāgasaṃyojanaṃ, avijjāsaṃyojanaṃ – imāni satta saṃyojanāni.

Herein, what are the seven fetters? The fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of craving for existence, and the fetter of ignorance—these are the seven fetters.

(3) Satta pariyuṭṭhānāni

(3) The Seven Assaults

Tattha katamāni satta pariyuṭṭhānāni? Kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhānaṃ, paṭighapariyuṭṭhānaṃ, mānapariyuṭṭhānaṃ, diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhānaṃ, vicikicchāpariyuṭṭhānaṃ, bhavarāgapariyuṭṭhānaṃ, avijjāpariyuṭṭhānaṃ – imāni satta pariyuṭṭhānāni.

Herein, what are the seven assaults? The assault of sensual lust, the assault of aversion, the assault of conceit, the assault of views, the assault of doubt, the assault of lust for existence, and the assault of ignorance—these are the seven assaults.

(4) Satta asaddhammā

(4) The Seven Unwholesome Principles

950. Tattha katame satta asaddhammā? Assaddho hoti, ahiriko hoti, anottappī hoti, appassuto hoti, kusīto hoti, muṭṭhassatī [T 0.0518] hoti, duppañño hoti – ime satta asaddhammā.

950. Herein, what are the seven unwholesome principles? One is faithless, is shameless, has no fear of wrongdoing, has little learning, is indolent, has lapsed mindfulness, and is unwise—these are the seven unwholesome principles.

(5) Satta duccaritāni

(5) The Seven Kinds of Misconduct

Tattha katamāni satta duccaritāni? Pāṇātipāto, adinnādānaṃ, kāmesumicchācāro, musāvādo, pisuṇā vācā, pharusā vācā, samphappalāpo – imāni satta duccaritāni.

Herein, what are the seven kinds of misconduct? Taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter—these are the seven kinds of misconduct.

(6) Satta mānā

(6) The Seven Kinds of Conceit

Tattha katame satta mānā? Māno, atimāno, mānātimāno, omāno, adhimāno, asmimāno, micchāmāno – ime satta mānā.

Herein, what are the seven kinds of conceit? Conceit, excessive conceit, conceit upon conceit, self-deprecation, overestimation, the conceit “I am,” and wrong conceit—these are the seven kinds of conceit.

(7) Satta diṭṭhiyo

(7) The Seven Kinds of Views

951. (Ka) tattha [V 0.0450] katamā satta diṭṭhiyo? Idhekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī hoti evaṃdiṭṭhi – “yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā rūpī [M 0.0398] cātumahābhūtiko cātummahābhūtiko (sī. syā.) mātāpettikasambhavo kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.

951. (a) Herein, what are the seven kinds of views? Here, some ascetic or brahmin holds such a doctrine, such a view: “Sirs, since this self—which is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father—is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to this extent, sirs, this self is completely annihilated.” In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.

(Kha) tamañño evamāha – “atthi kho, bho, eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi. ‘Neso natthī’ti vadāmi. No ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho bho añño attā dibbo rūpī kāmāvacaro kabaḷīkārabhakkho. Taṃ [P 0.0384] tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammāsamucchinno hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ [T 0.0519] paññapenti.

(b) Another says to him thus: “Sirs, that self of which you speak does indeed exist. I do not say, ‘It does not exist.’ But, sirs, this self is not completely annihilated to that extent. There is, sirs, another self that is divine, material, belonging to the sense-sphere, and subsisting on physical food. You do not know it or see it, but I know it and see it. Since that self, sirs, is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to this extent, sirs, this self is completely annihilated.” In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.

(Ga) tamañño evamāha – “atthi kho, bho, eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi. ‘Neso natthī’ti vadāmi. No ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho, bho, añño attā dibbo rūpī manomayo sabbaṅgapaccaṅgī ahīnindriyo. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.

(c) Another says to him thus: “Sirs, that self of which you speak does indeed exist. I do not say, ‘It does not exist.’ But, sirs, this self is not completely annihilated to that extent. There is, sirs, another self that is divine, material, mind-made, complete with all major and minor limbs, and possessing faculties that are not deficient. You do not know it or see it, but I know it and see it. Since that self, sirs, is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to this extent, sirs, this self is completely annihilated.” In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.

(Gha) tamañño evamāha – “atthi kho, bho, eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi. ‘Neso natthī’ti vadāmi. No ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho, bho, añño attā sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ananto ākāsoti ākāsānañcāyatanūpago. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati [V 0.0451] vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.

(d) Another says to him thus: “Sirs, that self of which you speak does indeed exist. I do not say, ‘It does not exist.’ But, sirs, this self is not completely annihilated to that extent. There is, sirs, another self that, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, percipient of ‘space is infinite,’ has attained the base of infinite space. You do not know it or see it, but I know it and see it. Since that self, sirs, is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to this extent, sirs, this self is completely annihilated.” In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.

(Ṅa) tamañño [M 0.0399] evamāha – “atthi kho, bho, eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi. ‘Neso natthī’ti vadāmi. No ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho, bho, añño attā sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma anantaṃ viññāṇanti viññāṇañcāyatanūpago. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.

(e) Another says to him thus: “Sirs, that self of which you speak does indeed exist. I do not say, ‘It does not exist.’ But, sirs, this self is not completely annihilated to that extent. There is, sirs, another self that, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, percipient of ‘consciousness is infinite,’ has attained the base of infinite consciousness. You do not know it or see it, but I know it and see it. Since that self, sirs, is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to this extent, sirs, this self is completely annihilated.” In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.

(Ca) tamañño evamāha – “atthi kho, bho, eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi. ‘Neso natthī’ti vadāmi. No ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho, bho, añño attā sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma natthi kiñcīti ākiñcaññāyatanūpago. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ [P 0.0385] jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.

(f) Another says to him thus: “Sirs, that self of which you speak does indeed exist. I do not say, ‘It does not exist.’ But, sirs, this self is not completely annihilated to that extent. There is, sirs, another self that, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, percipient of ‘there is nothing,’ has attained the base of nothingness. You do not know it or see it, but I know it and see it. Since that self, sirs, is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to this extent, sirs, this self is completely annihilated.” In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.

(Cha) tamañño evamāha – “atthi kho pana eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi. ‘Neso natthī’ti vadāmi. No ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho, bho, añño attā sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpago. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ [T 0.0521] attā sammā samucchinno hotī”ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti. Imā satta diṭṭhiyo.

(g) Another says to him: “Sirs, that self you speak of does exist—I do not say it does not. But, sirs, that self is not completely annihilated to that extent. There is, sirs, another self that, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. You do not know it or see it, but I know it and see it. Since that self, sirs, is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to this extent, sirs, this self is completely annihilated.” In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being. These are the seven views.

Sattakaṃ.

The Section of Sevens.

8. Aṭṭhakaniddeso

8. The Exposition of the Eights

(1) Aṭṭha kilesavatthūni

(1) Eight Bases of Defilement

952. Tattha [V 0.0452] katamāni aṭṭha kilesavatthūni? Lobho, doso, moho, māno, diṭṭhi, vicikicchā, thinaṃ, uddhaccaṃ – imāni aṭṭha kilesavatthūni.

952. Herein, what are the eight bases of defilement? Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, and restlessness—these are the eight bases of defilement.

(2) Aṭṭha kusītavatthūni

(2) Eight Grounds for Laziness

953. Tattha [M 0.0400] katamāni aṭṭha kusītavatthūni?

953. Herein, what are the eight grounds for laziness?

(Ka) idha bhikkhunā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “kammaṃ kho me kātabbaṃ bhavissati. Kammaṃ kho pana me karontassa kāyo kilamissati. Handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”ti. So nipajjati; na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā, anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ kusītavatthu.

Here, a bhikkhu has work to be done. It occurs to him: “Indeed, I will have work to do. While I am doing the work, my body will become tired. Well then, I shall lie down.” So he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. This is the first ground for laziness.

(Kha) puna caparaṃ bhikkhunā kammaṃ kataṃ hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “ahaṃ kho kammaṃ akāsiṃ. Kammaṃ kho pana me karontassa kāyo kilanto. Handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”ti. So nipajjati; na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā, anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu has done work. It occurs to him: “Indeed, I have done work. Having done the work, my body is tired. Well then, I shall lie down.” So he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. This is the second ground for laziness.

(Ga) puna caparaṃ bhikkhunā maggo gantabbo hoti. Tassa evaṃ [P 0.0386] hoti – “maggo kho me gantabbo bhavissati. Maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantassa kāyo kilamissati. Handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”ti. So nipajjati; na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā, anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu has a journey to make. It occurs to him: “Indeed, I will have a journey to make. While I am going on the journey, my body will become tired. Well then, I shall lie down.” So he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. This is the third ground for laziness.

(Gha) puna caparaṃ bhikkhunā [T 0.0522] maggo gato hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “ahaṃ kho maggaṃ agamāsiṃ. Maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantassa kāyo kilanto. Handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”ti. So nipajjati[V 0.0453]; na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā, anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ catutthaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu has gone on a journey. It occurs to him: “Indeed, I have gone on a journey. Having gone on the journey, my body is tired. Well then, I shall lie down.” So he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. This is the fourth ground for laziness.

(Ṅa) puna caparaṃ bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto na labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto nālatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa me kāyo kilanto akammañño. Handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”ti. So nipajjati; na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā, anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ pañcamaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu, while wandering for alms in a village or a town, does not obtain a satisfying amount of coarse or fine food. It occurs to him: “While wandering for alms in a village or a town, I did not obtain a satisfying amount of coarse or fine food. This body of mine is tired and unfit for work. Well then, I shall lie down.” So he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. This is the fifth ground for laziness.

(Ca) puna caparaṃ bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto alatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā [M 0.0401] bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa me kāyo kilanto akammañño māsācitaṃ maññe. Handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”ti. So nipajjati; na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā, anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu, while wandering for alms in a village or a town, obtains a satisfying amount of coarse or fine food. It occurs to him: “While wandering for alms in a village or a town, I obtained a satisfying amount of coarse or fine food. This body of mine is tired and unfit for work; I feel as if it is soaked like a bean. Well then, I shall lie down.” So he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. This is the sixth ground for laziness.

(Cha) puna caparaṃ bhikkhuno uppanno hoti appamattako ābādho. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “uppanno kho me ayaṃ appamattako ābādho. Atthi kappo nipajjituṃ[T 0.0523]. Handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”ti. So nipajjati; na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā, anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ sattamaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu has a minor illness. It occurs to him: “This minor illness has arisen in me. It is a suitable occasion to lie down. Well then, I shall lie down.” So he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. This is the seventh ground for laziness.

(Ja) puna caparaṃ bhikkhu gilānā vuṭṭhito gilānavuṭṭhito (saddanībhi) a. ni. 6.16 pāḷiyā ṭīkā passitabbā hoti aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “ahaṃ kho gilānā vuṭṭhito aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā. Tassa me kāyo dubbalo akammañño. Handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”ti. So nipajjati; na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā, anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ kusītavatthu. Imāni aṭṭha kusītavatthūni.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu has recovered from illness, being not long recovered from his sickness. It occurs to him: “I have recovered from illness, being not long recovered from my sickness. This body of mine is weak and unfit for work. Well then, I shall lie down.” So he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. This is the eighth ground for laziness. These are the eight grounds for laziness.

(3) Aṭṭhasu lokadhammesu cittassa paṭighāto

(3) Conflict in the mind regarding the eight worldly conditions

954. Tattha [P 0.0387][V 0.0454] katamesu aṭṭhasu lokadhammesu cittassa paṭighāto? Lābhe sārāgo, alābhe paṭivirodho, yase sārāgo, ayase paṭivirodho, pasaṃsāya sārāgo, nindāya paṭivirodho, sukhe sārāgo, dukkhe paṭivirodho – imesu aṭṭhasu lokadhammesu cittassa paṭighāto.

954. Herein, regarding which eight worldly conditions does conflict in the mind occur? Passionate attachment to gain, and opposition to loss; passionate attachment to status, and opposition to lack of status; passionate attachment to praise, and opposition to blame; passionate attachment to pleasure, and opposition to pain—regarding these eight worldly conditions, conflict in the mind occurs.

(4) Aṭṭhaanariyavohārā

(4) The Eight Ignoble Expressions

955. Tattha katame aṭṭha anariyavohārā? Adiṭṭhe diṭṭhavāditā, assute sutavāditā, amute mutavāditā, aviññāte viññātavāditā, diṭṭhe adiṭṭhavāditā, sute assutavāditā, mute amutavāditā, viññāte aviññātavāditā – ime aṭṭha anariyavohārā.

955. Herein, what are the eight ignoble expressions? Regarding the unseen, to speak of it as seen; regarding the unheard, to speak of it as heard; regarding the unsensed, to speak of it as sensed; regarding the uncognized, to speak of it as cognized. Regarding the seen, to speak of it as unseen; regarding the heard, to speak of it as unheard; regarding the sensed, to speak of it as unsensed; regarding the cognized, to speak of it as uncognized. These are the eight ignoble expressions.

(5) Aṭṭha micchattā

(5) The Eight Wrongnesses

956. Tattha katame aṭṭha micchattā? Micchādiṭṭhi, micchāsaṅkappo, micchāvācā, micchākammanto, micchāājīvo, micchāvāyāmo, micchāsati, micchāsamādhi – ime aṭṭha micchattā.

956. Herein, what are the eight wrongnesses? Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. These are the eight wrongnesses.

(6) Aṭṭha purisadosā

(6) The Eight Faults of a Person

957. Tattha [T 0.0524][M 0.0402] katame aṭṭha purisadosā? (Ka) idha bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ āpattiyā codenti. So bhikkhu bhikkhūhi āpattiyā codiyamāno codiyamāno (sī. syā.) a. ni. 8.14 “na sarāmi na sarāmī”ti assatiyāva nibbeṭheti. Ayaṃ paṭhamo purisadoso.

957. Herein, what are the eight faults of a person? Here, bhikkhus charge a bhikkhu with an offense. That bhikkhu, being charged with an offense by the bhikkhus, evades it simply through lack of recollection, saying, “I do not recollect, I do not recollect.” This is the first fault of a person.

(Kha) puna caparaṃ bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ āpattiyā codenti. So bhikkhu bhikkhūhi āpattiyā codiyamāno codakaṃyeva paṭippharati – “kiṃ nu kho tuyhaṃ bālassa abyattassa bhaṇitena! Tvampi nāma maṃ bhaṇitabbaṃ maññasī”ti! Ayaṃ dutiyo purisadoso.

Furthermore, bhikkhus charge a bhikkhu with an offense. That bhikkhu, being charged with an offense by the bhikkhus, retorts to the accuser himself: “Of what use is what is said by you, a fool, an incompetent one! Do you really think that you are one to admonish me?” This is the second fault of a person.

(Ga) puna [V 0.0455] caparaṃ bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ āpattiyā codenti. So bhikkhu bhikkhūhi āpattiyā codiyamāno codakaṃyeva codakasseva (syā.) a. ni. 8.14 paccāropeti – “tvampi khosi itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno. Tvaṃ tāva paṭhamaṃ paṭikarohī”ti. Ayaṃ tatiyo purisadoso.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused by monks of an offense, makes a counter-accusation against the accuser, saying, "You yourself have committed such-and-such an offense. You should first make amends for it." This is the third fault of a person.

(Gha) puna caparaṃ bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ āpattiyā codenti. So bhikkhu bhikkhūhi āpattiyā codiyamāno aññenāññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti. Ayaṃ catuttho purisadoso.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused by the monks of an offense, evades by changing the subject, diverts the talk to outside matters, and displays anger, ill will, and displeasure. This is the fourth fault of a person.

(Ṅa) puna caparaṃ bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ āpattiyā codenti. So bhikkhu [P 0.0388] bhikkhūhi āpattiyā codiyamāno saṅghamajjhe bāhāvikkhepakaṃ bhaṇati. Ayaṃ pañcamo purisadoso.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, speaks while waving his arms about in the midst of the Saṅgha. This is the fifth fault of a person.

(Ca) puna caparaṃ bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ āpattiyā codenti. So bhikkhu bhikkhūhi āpattiyā codiyamāno anādiyitvā saṅghaṃ, anādiyitvā codakaṃ, sāpattikova āpattikova (ka.) a. ni. 8.14 yenakāmaṃ pakkamati. Ayaṃ chaṭṭho purisadoso.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused by the monks of an offense, disregarding the Saṅgha and disregarding the accuser, departs as he pleases while still under the offense. This is the sixth fault of a person.

(Cha) puna caparaṃ bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ āpattiyā codenti. So bhikkhu bhikkhūhi āpattiyā codiyamāno “nevāhaṃ āpannomhi, na panāhaṃ anāpannomhī”ti tuṇhībhūto saṅghaṃ viheseti. Ayaṃ [T 0.0525] sattamo purisadoso.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused by the monks of an offense, vexes the Saṅgha by remaining silent. This is the seventh fault of a person.

(Ja) puna caparaṃ bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ āpattiyā codenti. So bhikkhu bhikkhūhi āpattiyā codiyamāno evamāha – “kiṃ nu kho tumhe āyasmanto atibāḷhaṃ [M 0.0403] mayi byāvaṭā. Idānāhaṃ sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattissāmī”ti. So sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattitvā evamāha – “idāni kho tumhe āyasmanto attamanā hothā”ti. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo purisadoso. Ime aṭṭha purisadosā.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused by the monks of an offense, says, "Why are you venerables so intensely concerned with me? Now I will renounce the training and return to the lower life." Having renounced the training and returned to the lower life, he says, "Now, venerables, you should be pleased." This is the eighth fault of a person. These are the eight faults of a person.

(7) Aṭṭha asaññīvādā

The Eight Doctrines of Non-Perception

958. Tattha katame aṭṭha asaññīvādā? “Rūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – asaññīti naṃ paññapenti; arūpī attā…pe… rūpī ca arūpī ca…pe… nevarūpīnārūpī…pe… “antavā attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – asaññīti naṃ paññapenti; “anantavā attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – asaññīti naṃ paññapenti; “antavā [P 0.0389] ca anantavā ca attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – asaññīti naṃ paññapenti; “nevantavā nānantavā attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – asaññīti naṃ paññapenti. Ime aṭṭha asaññīvādā.

958. Herein, what are the eight doctrines of non-perception? 'The self has form and is constant after death'—they designate it as non-percipient; 'The self is formless...' and so on... 'The self is both with and without form...' and so on... 'The self is neither with nor without form...' and so on... 'The self is finite and is constant after death'—they designate it as non-percipient; 'The self is infinite and is constant after death'—they designate it as non-percipient; 'The self is both finite and infinite and is constant after death'—they designate it as non-percipient; 'The self is neither finite nor infinite and is constant after death'—they designate it as non-percipient. These are the eight doctrines of non-perception.

(8) Aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā

The Eight Doctrines of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception

959. Tattha katame aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā? “Rūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti [V 0.0456] – nevasaññīnāsaññīti [T 0.0526] naṃ paññapenti; “arūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – nevasaññīnāsaññīti naṃ paññapenti; “rūpī ca arūpī ca attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – nevasaññīnāsaññīti naṃ paññapenti; “nevarūpīnārūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – nevasaññīnāsaññīti naṃ paññapenti; “antavā attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – nevasaññīnāsaññīti naṃ paññapenti; “anantavā attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – nevasaññīnāsaññīti naṃ paññapenti; “antavā ca anantavā ca attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – nevasaññīnāsaññīti naṃ paññapenti; “nevantavā nānantavā attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti – nevasaññīnāsaññīti naṃ paññapenti. Ime aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā.

959. Herein, what are the eight doctrines of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? 'The self has form and is constant after death'—they declare it to be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. 'The self is formless and is constant after death'—they declare it to be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. 'The self is both with and without form and is constant after death'—they declare it to be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. 'The self is neither with nor without form and is constant after death'—they declare it to be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. 'The self is finite and is constant after death'—they declare it to be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. 'The self is infinite and is constant after death'—they declare it to be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. 'The self is both finite and infinite and is constant after death'—they declare it to be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. 'The self is neither finite nor infinite and is constant after death'—they declare it to be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. These are the eight doctrines of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Aṭṭhakaṃ.

The Section on Eights.

9. Navakaniddeso

9. The Exposition of the Nines

(1) Nava āghātavatthūni

The Nine Bases for Resentment

960. Tattha katamāni nava āghātavatthūni? “Anatthaṃ me acarī”ti āghāto jāyati[V 0.0457]; “anatthaṃ me caratī”ti āghāto jāyati; “anatthaṃ [M 0.0404] me carissatī”ti āghāto jāyati; “piyassa me manāpassa anatthaṃ acari”…pe… anatthaṃ carati…pe… anatthaṃ carissatīti āghāto jāyati; appiyassa me amanāpassa atthaṃ acari…pe… atthaṃ carati…pe… atthaṃ carissatīti āghāto jāyati. Imāni nava āghātavatthūni.

960. Herein, what are the nine bases for resentment? Resentment arises, thinking: “He has done me harm.” Resentment arises, thinking: “He is doing me harm.” Resentment arises, thinking: “He will do me harm.” Resentment arises, thinking: “He has done harm to someone dear and agreeable to me”... and so on... “he is doing harm”... and so on... “he will do harm.” Resentment arises, thinking: “He has done good to someone disliked and disagreeable to me”... and so on... “he is doing good”... and so on... “he will do good.” These are the nine bases for resentment.

(2) Nava purisamalāni

The Nine Impurities of a Person

961. Tattha katamāni nava purisamalāni? Kodho, makkho, issā, macchariyaṃ, māyā, sāṭheyyaṃ, musāvādo, pāpicchatā, micchādiṭṭhi – imāni nava purisamalāni.

961. Herein, what are the nine impurities of a person? Anger, contempt, envy, avarice, deceit, craftiness, false speech, evil desires, and wrong view—these are the nine impurities of a person.

(3) Navavidhā mānā

The Nine Types of Conceit

962. Tattha [T 0.0527] katame navavidhā mānā? “Seyyassa seyyohamasmī”ti māno, “seyyassa [P 0.0390] sadisohamasmī”ti māno, “seyyassa hīnohamasmī”ti māno, “sadisassa seyyohamasmī”ti māno, “sadisassa sadisohamasmī”ti māno, “sadisassa hīnohamasmī”ti māno, “hīnassa seyyohamasmī”ti māno, “hīnassa sadisohamasmī”ti māno, “hīnassa hīnohamasmī”ti māno – ime navavidhā mānā.

962. Herein, what are the nine types of conceit? The conceit: “I am better than one who is superior,” the conceit: “I am equal to one who is superior,” the conceit: “I am inferior to one who is superior,” the conceit: “I am better than one who is equal,” the conceit: “I am equal to one who is equal,” the conceit: “I am inferior to one who is equal,” the conceit: “I am better than one who is inferior,” the conceit: “I am equal to one who is inferior,” the conceit: “I am inferior to one who is inferior”—these are the nine types of conceit.

(4) Nava taṇhāmūlakā dhammā

The Nine Qualities Rooted in Craving

963. Tattha katame nava taṇhāmūlakā dhammā? Taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā, pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho, lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo, vinicchayaṃ paṭicca chandarāgo, chandarāgaṃ paṭicca ajjhosānaṃ, ajjhosānaṃ paṭicca pariggaho, pariggahaṃ paṭicca macchariyaṃ, macchariyaṃ paṭicca ārakkho, ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ daṇḍādāna-satthādāna-kalaha-viggahavivāda-tuvaṃtuvaṃ-pesuñña-musāvādā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavanti – ime nava taṇhāmūlakā dhammā.

963. Herein, what are the nine qualities rooted in craving? Dependent on craving, there is seeking; dependent on seeking, there is gain; dependent on gain, there is decision; dependent on decision, there is desire and lust; dependent on desire and lust, there is attachment; dependent on attachment, there is possessiveness; dependent on possessiveness, there is stinginess; dependent on stinginess, there is guarding. On account of guarding, many evil, unwholesome qualities arise: taking up sticks and weapons, quarrels, conflicts, disputes, contention, divisive speech, and false speech. These are the nine qualities rooted in craving.

(5) Nava iñjitāni

(5) Nine Agitations

964.
